report.answer_text:
Sanae Takaichi became prime minister in October 2025. Her main economic proposals that year were these:
"Responsible proactive fiscal policy"
She described her approach as "responsible proactive fiscal policy"[1]. Commentators have compared it to Abenomics, with aggressive fiscal spending and easing[2].
On debt, she argued that if debt grows more slowly than the economy, financial sustainability will be secured[3].
¥21.3 trillion stimulus package (approved November 21)
The Cabinet approved a ¥21.3 trillion ($136 billion) package.[4] It is the largest since the pandemic.[4]
It includes ¥17.7 trillion of spending, ¥2.7 trillion in tax breaks and ¥900 billion in special account spending.[4]
It rests on three priorities: relief from the rising cost of living; "strategic investments" in shipbuilding, AI and semiconductors; and higher defense spending, bringing total defense expenditures for FY2025 to 2% of GDP.[5]
Cost-of-living measures include scrapping a provisional gasoline tax and expanding subsidies for electricity and gas bills.[6]
A supplementary budget is needed to fund it. Because she leads a minority government, she needs opposition cooperation to pass it.[7]
Growth and structural policy
She announced a Growth Strategy Council to map out policies for innovation, industrial revitalization, and "crisis management investments" in areas such as food security.[3]
She also reiterated a commitment to making Japan a leading global asset management hub and creating a national disaster-prevention agency.[3]
Monetary policy
A draft outline said the package would urge the Bank of Japan to focus on strong economic growth with stable prices, reflecting her preference for low interest rates.[8]
Reception
Markets reacted with concern. The package stoked fears about Japan's debt, sending government bond yields to record highs and the yen lower.[9]
Opposition lawmakers and experts have questioned whether the package will be effective.[7]
Supporters point to the Cabinet Office estimate that it would raise GDP by 24 trillion yen.[7]
If you'd like, I can look at how things have developed since then. For example, the package's actual effects, or the Bank of Japan's response.
